rationale: Round 1 built and ran cleanly, so this candidate raises security/diversity pressure across the board. SUB gets the strongest weights because flops-6 is dense floating-point arithmetic where instruction substitution adds real reverse-engineering friction at near-zero runtime and size cost. FLA and BCF are pushed higher than round 1 to obscure the hot-loop control flow — the small 753-byte main body can absorb the size blowup, and BCF's CorrectnessRisk stays modestly weighted since round 1 showed no issues. SPLIT remains cheap and is kept high because it enlarges the block pool that makes FLA and BCF more effective. IBR and ICALL are raised moderately: indirect branching/calls hinder static analysis but carry real dispatch overhead in a FLOPS-bound kernel, so their RuntimeCost weights stay elevated to keep them off the hottest loops. IGV is kept mid-range since the program has few globals and its benefit is limited, while runtime/size/correctness cost weights across all passes remain non-trivial so the feature-driven selector still de-escalates passes on the tightest FP kernels, preserving the benchmark's runtime envelope and correctness (as verified in round 1).
